title: 'Stripped naked and brutally attacked': Family sues over mentally ill man's death inside Toronto jail
subtitle: Ibrahim Ali was initially arrested over a pack of cigarettes, allegedly stolen from an Etobicoke convenience store.
article: The family of a mentally ill man who died after being "stripped naked and brutally attacked by his cellmate" inside a Toronto jail has launched a wrongful death lawsuit against the province.

It's the latest case to highlight the crowded and sometimes dangerous conditions at the Toronto South Detention Centre - particularly for people like Ibrahim Ali, who must manage mental illnesses while awaiting trial in jail.
Ali's case began with a pack of cigarettes, allegedly stolen from an Etobicoke convenience store.

After Ali's arrest, the statement of claim, filed this month in Toronto, alleges the province violated his Charter rights by failing to take reasonable steps to protect his safety while in custody. It further alleges the facility failed to offer Ali adequate mental health services for his schizophrenia, and that it did not supervise his interactions with his cellmate, whom he'd told his family was also displaying signs of a psychiatric disorder.
After days on life-support, Ali was pronounced dead on April 29 at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto. He was 31.
"The public needs to know the truth about what happens" to people in the Toronto South, Ali's brother, Yusuf, wrote in a statement to the Star.
The family is seeking a minimum of $3 million in damages; their claims have not been tested in court.
A statement of defence has not been filed with the courts. When reached by the Star, the Ministry of the Solicitor General, which oversees Ontario's jails, declined to comment.
"It would be inappropriate to provide comment on this matter given it is before the court," said spokesperson Brent Ross.

In recent years, conditions at the facility, where more than 80 per cent of inmates are awaiting trial, have drawn sharp criticism not only from inmates and their loved ones, but from judicial officials within a number of court rulings.
Earlier this year, Euplio Cusano, a senior citizen with a brain injury, was killed in an attack inside his TSDC cell , after spending seven months in custody without a bail hearing.
In some cases, sentences for convicted offenders have been reduced over the amount spent time subject to the jail's "inhumane" conditions .

Ali was a bright kid who was accepted into each of the universities to which he applied, his family recalls. He ultimately chose to enrol in the chemical engineering program at what was then Ryerson University, now Toronto Metropolitan University.
But, nearing the finish line of his degree, Ali began to struggle with his mental health.
"He started to miss school a lot and (staying) secluded from everyone else," Yusuf wrote in the family's statement. "It got to the point where he wouldn't eat or sleep and he became paranoid."
Ali dropped out of school in his third year. From there, things continued to go downhill. "It got to the point where he wouldn't eat or sleep and he became paranoid," Yusuf said.
In 2014, at the age of 20, Ali was diagnosed with schizophrenia - a disorder that often manifests itself in early adulthood.

According to his family, Ali was able to manage his diagnosis with relative success for nearly a decade. While his family recalled several "non-violent encounters with police" over those years, each had been resolved by taking Ali to a mental health facility.

But in March 2023, Ali was arrested after allegedly stealing a pack of cigarettes from a convenience store near his family home in Etobicoke. Court documents obtained by the Star show his initial charges as one count each of theft and uttering threats.
Ali was initially released on conditions, but he struggled to navigate the criminal justice system, and ultimately chose to represent himself, his family said.

Out on bail, Ali continued to rack up criminal charges, including five more instances in which police say he attempted to steal packs of cigarettes and alcohol from retailers in Etobicoke and Toronto, along with a number of counts of failure to comply. In one incident, police allege Ali was armed with a knife.
In October, Ali's bail was revoked and he was remanded into pre-trial detention at the Toronto South.

In several phone calls from inside the jail, Ali told his family he'd been assigned a cell with another individual whom he believed also had schizophrenia, the claim states, alleging this was negligence on the part of the province for failing to provide adequate mental health considerations to either Ali or his cellmate.
On April 21, 2024, the lawsuit alleges, Ali was "stripped naked" inside of his cell and "brutally attacked."

"The attack occurred in an approximate window of 40 minutes in which Ibrahim and his cellmate were unsupervised by TSDC staff, including staff responsible for monitoring video surveillance," it reads.
Once discovered by staff, Ali was transported to hospital.
Toronto police initially charged another inmate, Samuel El Hasheem, 27, with attempted murder; the charge was later upgraded to first-degree murder.
Ali's siblings rushed to the hospital the next day but, the claim states, correctional officers delayed their visit by nearly two hours until they agreed to undergo background checks.

Yusuf described the sight of his brother, who by then had slipped into a coma, as a "heartbreaking" situation made worse by the absence of Ali's parents, Kadhra and Abdi, who were thousands of kilometres away visiting family in Somalia when their son was attacked.
When Yusuf tried to FaceTime his parents from the hospital room, he said correctional officers told him photography and filming was prohibited.
"The next day, they stationed two guards in the room to keep an eye on our family to make sure we didn't use our phones while we were anywhere near our brother," he said.
Eventually, Yusuf said, the officers threatened to ban him from the hospital room if he continued to try to use his phone.

It took six days for Ali's parents to return from Somalia, a journey Yusuf says they spent "worrying endlessly" whether they would be able to see Ibrahim before he passed, "and if they should have even gone on the trip in the first place."
When they made it to St. Michael's, Ali was already brain dead, however doctors had held off on removing him from life support until the family could reunite.
Yusuf described his parents' reunion with Ali, unconscious in his hospital bed, as "one of the worst moments of their lives."
"They blame themselves even though being here wouldn't have changed the situation," he wrote.
In the eight months since Ali's death, his family says they've been given few answers; they heard from Toronto police once after the incident, they said, but not since.
"The Minister of the Solicitor General is even more unknown to us; we have not spoken to a single person from there."
The Office of the Chief Coroner has confirmed to the Star that an inquest into Ali's death will be mandatory, as is the case when any provincial inmate dies under non-natural circumstances.
According to lawyer Jeffrey Hartman, Ali's case should serve as a much-needed reminder that the rights of inmates are non-negotiable.

"People need to understand that it is not some form of benevolence to respect the human rights of the most vulnerable members of society, including prisoners," Hartman, representing the Alis, told the Star. "The reality is that Ibrahim did not fail us - we failed him through our collective intellectual laziness, which erodes our claim to be a rights-respecting culture."
